newsitem.title: USA: Best inflation news behind us - Atlanta Fed's Rogers.
newsitem.headline: Best inflation news behind us - Atlanta Fed's Rogers.

text.p: A six-year trend of lower U.S. inflation may be coming to an end, though only modest threats of faster price growth appear on the horizon, said Atlanta Federal Reserve Bank economist Mark Rogers.
Creeping wage pressure and higher energy prices should ultimately filter through the U.S. economy, stalling further inflation reduction, said Rogers in an interview with Reuters Financial Televsion.
"By saying the best news is behind us, I think prices will no longer be as soft, but ... we won't see the inflation picking up either," Rogers said.
The U.S. consumer price index growth rate has steadily fallen to below 3.0 percent from 6.1 percent in 1990, even as the economy has expanded continuously since mid-1991.

But the latest Atlanta Fed survey of local manufacturers released Tuesday showed expectations of higher raw materials prices ahead, which could ratchet up costs further along the production pipeline, Rogers noted.
"Looking ahead, they are not as optimistic about prices remaining this soft," Rogers said.
Still, Rogers played down the risks that inflation will accelerate rapidly in coming months.
Solid job gains in 1996 have pushed U.S. unemployment toward five percent, which has many economists sounding alarms of inflationary wage growth ahead.
But job growth may soon slow or even reverse, with many firms realizing the slowing economy could render some of their recent hires expendable, Rogers said.
"Employers are realizing that maybe earlier in the year they hired just a little more than they needed and there's room to play catch-up there," said Rogers.
Rogers cited a mixed bag of economic trends which suggest moderate growth at best in coming months.

"I think there's broad consensus that the overall economy is relatively healthy. Some deceleration, but still healthy in terms of consumer spending, business investment and even export growth," Rogers said.

The capacity utilization rate remains below 84 percent and the 85.5-percent cycle peak from January 1995, suggesting manufacturers have room to grow a bit more without stoking higher inflation, Rogers added.
"We are in a moderate growth phase. The key question is: at what level of capacity is the economy. We have seen moderate numbers in terms of capacity utilization," he said.
